passage: The house was full of drums that Friday, because Tanuja's cousin's wedding party had started early downstairs, but the physics exam was on Monday. Tanuja told herself she would revise as soon as things settled. First she answered forty messages in the class group. Then she replied to Sunaina about the poster colours, watered the balcony plants, folded the laundry and cleared her inbox down to zero. By nine the phone was quiet and the room felt tidy and finished. Under a pile of dupattas, the physics book was still shut. Tanuja looked at it and felt a small, heavy drop in her stomach. 😟

qa.q: What did Tanuja do before nine o'clock that evening?
qa.a: Tanuja answered forty messages in the class group, replied to Sunaina, watered the balcony plants, folded the laundry and cleared her inbox.

qa.q: What did Tanuja feel when she saw the shut physics book?
qa.a: A small heavy drop of worry in her stomach: the busy evening had felt productive, but the exam task was still untouched.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do at nine o'clock to protect the exam revision?
qa.a: Turn the phone face down, open the book and do one small chapter section first, before any more messages or chores.

qa.q: How does Sunaina's message about poster colours fit into the evening?
qa.a: It was one more loud, small request that Tanuja answered quickly, and answering it felt useful even though it did not move the physics revision forward.

grounding: A teenager answers every message and does small chores while the important exam revision slides.

passage: On the study table Thomas wrote a to-do list: sort desk, reply to Joseph, iron uniform, charge earphones, chemistry ch. 6 revision. He did the first four in order, ticking each one with a flourish, and felt like a man in charge. The desk was spotless. Joseph had replied twice with jokes, and Thomas answered both. Uniform pressed, earphones full. The clock said ten past nine. Chemistry, last on the list, was tomorrow's quiz on six pages he had not read. Thomas rubbed his eyes, opened the book and took one long breath. “Should have started with you,” he muttered, reading the first line twice.

qa.q: What was the last item on Thomas's to-do list?
qa.a: The last item on Thomas's list was chemistry chapter 6 revision.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel as he ticked off the first four jobs?
qa.a: Thomas felt capable and in charge; the tidy desk and the ticks gave him a sense of progress even though the important task was untouched.

qa.q: What could Thomas change about how he writes his list tomorrow?
qa.a: Put chemistry first and give it a fixed start time, leaving the desk, the uniform and the replies for after.

qa.q: How might Joseph see the delayed replies and jokes?
qa.a: Joseph probably sees someone chatting cheerfully, and does not know the jokes are taking time from Thomas's chemistry.

grounding: A teenager does small urgent tasks first while important revision keeps waiting.

passage: Sit, Shreya, and put that phone face down for a minute. When I was your age, fifteen, my board exams were eight weeks away. Your great-uncle Kishore and I shared a room. Every time a neighbour shouted for help carrying a gas cylinder, Kishore ran. He answered every letter, swept the steps, fixed the radio. He felt so busy, so useful. His history book stayed shut. Three weeks before the exam he sat on the bed and said, "I've done everything except the thing." He made a rule: history from six to eight each morning, errands after. He passed, just about. I still remember his face that day.

qa.q: How far away were the board exams when the story begins?
qa.a: The board exams were eight weeks away.

qa.q: What did Kishore feel when he said, "I've done everything except the thing"?
qa.a: He felt shaken and a little ashamed, realising all his busy helping had pushed his history book aside.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story turned things around for Kishore?
qa.a: His rule of history from six to eight each morning, with errands only after, protected the important work before the small jobs could crowd in.

qa.q: How might Shreya see this story?
qa.a: Shreya might recognise herself in it, since the elder asked her to put her phone face down before telling it.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who stays busy with small urgent jobs while important exam revision keeps slipping.

passage: The power cut came at seven, right when Darshan had finally opened his chemistry notes. He lit the emergency lamp, but its battery was low. Then his phone buzzed: Tanuja asking about the class trip money list. He replied. Then the group chat. Then his mother needed him to fetch water before the tank ran dry. Each thing took five minutes and felt like a win. At nine the lamp flickered out. Chemistry, the test on Thursday, had got fifteen minutes. Darshan sat in the dark, annoyed. Next evening he switched the phone off, charged the lamp and did chemistry before anything else.

qa.q: When did the power cut happen?
qa.a: The power cut came at seven.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when the lamp went out at nine?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and frustrated with himself, because chemistry had only got fifteen minutes while the small tasks had eaten the evening.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Every quick reply and small chore felt productive, so the test revision kept sliding; switching the phone off and doing chemistry first fixed it.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Darshan's quick reply?
qa.a: Tanuja probably sees him as helpful and reliable, with no idea that answering her cost him study time.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose messages and small chores feel productive while the important exam revision keeps getting postponed.

passage: Gurpreet's revision timetable was stuck on her bedroom door in Pune: physics, two hours, every afternoon. At four she sat down. Her phone lit up. Ankita wanted a photo of today's notes. Gurpreet sent it. Then she watered her mother's plants because they looked dry. Then she answered three more messages and rearranged her pen stand. By six she felt oddly busy and tired, and the physics chapter was on the same page. "Why is it so loud?" she muttered, looking at the phone. She put it in the kitchen drawer, set a timer for forty minutes and opened the book to page 112.

qa.q: Where was Gurpreet's revision timetable stuck?
qa.a: It was stuck on her bedroom door in Pune.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling at six o'clock?
qa.a: She felt oddly busy and tired but uneasy, because physics had not moved though she had been working all afternoon.

qa.q: Which step helped Gurpreet start revising?
qa.a: Putting the phone in the kitchen drawer and setting a forty-minute timer removed the noisy distractions and gave the revision a clear start.

qa.q: How is Ankita affected by Gurpreet's choices?
qa.a: Ankita gets the notes she wanted quickly, and she may not realise that her small request was one of many that pulled Gurpreet away from physics.

grounding: Illustrates urgent-feeling small tasks and messages crowding out quiet, important exam revision for a teenager.

passage:
"Saurabh, how's the physics revision going?"
"Going, Rashmi didi. I'll start in ten minutes."
"You said that at four."
"I had to reply to the class group. Someone asked about the tuition timing."
"And after that?"
"Mummy asked me to get milk. Then my bike chain came off, so I fixed it. Then the cricket group was arguing about Sunday's match…"
"And physics?"
"Physics is… open." He pointed at the book on the bed.
"Saurabh, the exam is in nine days. How many chapters are left?"
"Six."
"Every one of those messages felt urgent, right?"
"Yes! People were waiting."
"Nobody's waiting on physics. It doesn't ping. That's why it keeps sliding."
He looked at his phone. It buzzed again. He turned it face down.
"Okay. Phone in the kitchen for an hour?"
"I'll hold it hostage," she said, holding out her hand. He gave it to her.

qa.q: How many chapters of physics are left?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel about all the messages and small jobs?
qa.a: Saurabh felt they were urgent and productive, as if people were waiting on him, even while physics slid.

qa.q: What small step helped Saurabh get to the important task?
qa.a: Putting his phone in the kitchen with Rashmi didi for an hour, so the loud urgent things could not interrupt.

qa.q: How does Rashmi didi see Saurabh's afternoon?
qa.a: Rashmi didi sees that the quiet, important revision keeps losing to noisy small things, and she steps in with humour to help.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose messages and small chores feel urgent while exam revision keeps sliding.
